full_judgment:
Mr. Syed Refaat Ahmed, J:- In this Application under Article 102 of the Constitution a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the arbitrary assessment of the goods covered under L/C number 074211010387 dated. 20.11.2011 lying under B/E No. C-3489 dated 9.1.2012 on the basis of CRF No. BV111ff 862 dated 14.12.2011 (Annexure-'D') showing price of the imported goods at higher inflated rate ignoring the transaction value should not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and of no legal effect and as to why the Respondents shall not be directed to assess the Petitioner's goods on the basis of the transaction value as per Section 25(1) and (2) of the Customs Act, 1969 ("the Act") read with the Customs Valuation (Fixing the price of imported goods) Rules, 2000 ("the Rules") and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The Petitioner, being an industrial concern, opened Letter of Credit ("L/C") to import electrolytic copper rod ("Goods") as raw material for its industry. The initial Pro forma Invoice ("PI") for the "L/C" was based on London Metal Exchange (LME) price of that day. As per international norms and procedure for procuring such goods, the Petitioner and its supplier upon negotiation, finalized the deal and 'Locked in' the price of that date's LME price and accordingly revised the L/C. Goods being mandated for pre shipment inspection, M/S Bureau Veritas ("PSI Agent"), at the time of PSI, issued the Clean Report Finding ("CRF") with approximately 30% additional valuation over the invoice value. The Petitioner contends that no prior enquiry was made by the PSI Agent prior to increasing the invoice valuation. However, the Petitioner immediately wrote to the PSI Agent requesting revision and the PSI Agent wrote back affirming that the valuation was undertaken under Rule 6 of the Rules. 

 3. Upon arrival of the Goods in Bangladesh, the Bill of Entry was issued and the Goods were assessed based on the CRF value and the Petitioner wrote to the Respondent No.1 Commissioner of Customs requesting to accept bank guarantee for the difference between the CRF value and the transaction value. Not having received any reply to its request, Petitioner initiated the instant Writ proceeding against the Respondents. 

 4. It is noted that at or around the time of importation of the Goods, the Petitioner also imported four other consignments of same raw material approximately in the same quantity. The first three of such consignments were also assessed arbitrarily but the Petitioner had to release these (with a view to maintaining industrial production) on the basis of CRF valuation. However, the Petitioner went before the Review Committee as per the Pre-shipment Inspection Rules, 2012 the ("PSI Rules") and all three of the respective CRFs were decided to have been wrongfully issued. The Review Committee in all three instances found instead that the appropriate assessment should have been based on invoice value. Subsequent to initiation of this Writ proceeding, a fifth consignment was assessed by the PSI Agent in accordance with the invoice value that is consistent with LME valuation and incidentally happens to be approximately 30% lesser than the CRF valuation of the Goods. 

 5. The instant Writ Petition also raises for this Court's consideration the issue of the Respondents' failure to assess and release the Goods, upon accepting a bank guarantee/undertaking in accordance with Rule. 22(4) of the PSI Rules and why such failure should not be declared to have been without lawful authority and of no legal effect and why the Respondents resultantly shall not be directed to assess and release the Goods imported by the Petitioner under Bill of Entry No. C-3489 dated 9.1.2012 on the basis of the declared invoice value within a stipulated period of time. 

 6. The issues before this Court, therefore, are whether the Respondent No. 7 PSI Agent rightfully assessed and issued the CRF in question and whether the Respondents in the facts acted illegally by not accepting a bank guarantee for the difference of the CRF value and transaction value of the Goods. 

 7. In determining these issues this Court has had reference to the international legal standards on Customs valuation that have found due incorporation in Bangladesh's municipal law. In this regard, reference material placed for this Court's consideration by the learned Advocate for the Petitioner Mr. Sajed Ahammad Sami include the Brief Guide to The Customs Valuation Agreement (World Customs Organization; Third Edition: August 1996) and Technical Information on Customs Valuation. It suffices to note at the outset that the customs valuation mechanism as has developed in Bangladesh is heavily indebted to and dependent on these international standards, a fact that, as we shall see, is found readily acknowledged in the relevant municipal law. 

 8. As submitted by Mr. Sami, a good point to start at understanding the scheme of the law in this regard would be the Act itself. Under section 25A of the Act, the Government appointed pre-shipment agencies or PSI Agents undertake assessment of goods that are imported into Bangladesh. Section 25B of the Act makes it mandatory for all goods to be inspected and assessed by such PSI agents, unless goods of a class is exempted from this requirement. Section 25A (2) of Act further stipulates that valuation verified and certified by a PSI Agent in accordance with the prescribed manner shall be the basis of assessment for import duty. Section 25A (3) refers to Section 25 (1) and (2) of the Act with regards to 'price' Section 25(1) provides for detailed assessment criteria for customs duty on the basis of valuation of goods, emphasizing on their actual price, i.e., price actually paid or payable. Section 25 (2) empowers the Government to promulgate necessary rules under which price of imported goods shall be determined having consideration to the criteria laid down in Section 25(1). It is deduced, therefore, from a reading of these provisions that the Act provides for the following regulatory and implementation framework: 

 (a) Assessment of value of imported goods based on the price actually paid or payable; 

 (b) Authority to promulgate of detailed rules for determining value of imported goods; and 

 It is noted that Customs duties can be the designated in either specific or ad valorem terms or as a mix of the two. In case of a specific duty, a concrete sum is charged for a quantitative description of the goods, for example US$ 1 per item or per unit. The Customs value of the goods does not need to be determined, as the duty is not based on the value of the goods but on other criteria. In this case, no rules on Customs valuation are needed and the Valuation Agreement does not apply. In contrast, an ad valorem duty depends on the value of the goods. 

 It is therefore evidently the case that Customs valuation is a Customs procedure applied to determine the Customs value of imported goods. If the rate of duty is ad valorem, the Customs value is essential to determine the duty to be paid on an imported good. To be considered in that context is the fact that Article VII of the GATT 1994 lays down the general principles for an international system of valuation. It stipulates that the value for customs purposes of imported merchandise should be based on the actual value of the imported merchandise on which duty is assessed, or of like merchandise, and should not be based on the value of merchandise of national origin or on arbitrary or fictitious values. 

 10. The Tokyo Round Valuation Code, or the Agreement on Implementation of Article VII of the GATT, concluded in 1979, established a positive system of Customs valuation based on the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods. Based on "transaction value", as distinct from the "notional value", it was intended to provide a fair, uniform and neutral system for the valuation of goods for customs purposes, conforming to commercial realities. The Tokyo Round Code was replaced by the WTO Agreement on Implementation of Article VII of the GATT 1994 following conclusion of the Uruguay Round. This Valuation Agreement is essentially the same as the Tokyo Round Valuation Code and applies only to the valuation of imported goods for the purpose of levying ad valorem duties on such goods. The Valuation Agreement stipulates that Customs valuation shall, except in specified circumstances, be based on the actual price of the goods to be valued, which is generally shown on the invoice. This price, plus adjustments for certain elements listed in Article 8 of the Agreement, equals the "transaction value", which constitutes the first, fundamental and most important method of valuation referred to in the said Agreement. Furthermore, for cases in which there is no "transaction value", or where the "transaction value" is not acceptable as the Customs value because the price has been distorted as a result of certain conditions, the Agreement lays down five other methods of Customs valuation, to be applied strictly in the prescribed hierarchical or sequential order. Overall the following six methods are considered in the Valuation Agreement: 

 Method 1: transaction value 

 Method 2: transaction value of identical goods 

 Method 3: transaction value of similar goods 

 Article VII of the GATT 1994, or the Valuation Agreement, therefore, provides for the international law governing Customs valuation. The primary basis for Customs value under this Agreement is "transaction value" as defined in Article 1. Article 1 is to be read together with Article 8 which provides, inter alia, for adjustments to the price actually paid or payable in cases where certain specific elements which are considered to form a part of the value for Customs purposes are incurred by the buyer but are not included in the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods. Article 1 incorporating the basic principle of Customs valuation relevantly reads thus: 

 "The Customs value of imported goods shall he the transaction value, that is the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to the country of importation adjusted in accordance with the provisions of Article 8..." 

 11. This Court notes that Rule 3 of the Valuation Rules, similarly also stipulates that "transaction value" shall be the basis of assessment of Customs duties and "transaction value" as envisaged in Rule 4 (read with Rule 10) of the Valuation Rules. Citing pertinently the WTO Technical Information on Customs Valuation, Mr. Sami reiterates that the basic principle of determining "transaction value" under the Valuation Agreement or Article VII of the GATT 1994, therefore, is the value to be paid or payable, generally shown on the invoice, subject to necessary adjustments. He further satisfactorily submits that in the event "transaction value" is not possible to determine, the Valuation Agreement lays down five other methods of Customs valuation, to be applied in the prescribed hierarchical or sequential order as already above noted. Referring to the Brief on Customs Valuation, as published by Directorate General of Valuation, India, Mr. Sami draws this Court's attention to that fact that in India, which is a founding member of the GATT (presently the WTO), the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 follows the same methods laid down by Article VII of the GATT 1994 as enumerated above. Under the said rules "transaction value" is also the primary method of assessment of valuation, where the invoice value, subject to certain valuation factors is the basis of "transaction value". Therefore, Rule 3(i) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 states that the value of imported goods shall be the transaction value. Rule 4(i) thereof defines "transaction value" as the price actually paid or payable for goods (i.e., the invoice value) when sold for export to India adjusted in accordance with the provisions of Rule 9 therein. The 1988 Rules further provides that in the event that the "transaction value" method is not applicable, goods shall be valued by applying the subsequent methods in a strictly hierarchical order. 

 12. This Court finds that the Valuation Rules also reflects the above principles where, under Rule 4, "transaction value" is defined as the actual price paid or payable, subject to adjustments made under Rule 10. If it is, however, not possible to determine "transaction value", then by the terms of Rule 3 (M), Rules 5,6,7,8, and 9 are to be applied in sequential order to determine the value of such imported goods. Under Rule 5 of the Valuation Rules, the transaction value of "identical goods", imported into Bangladesh at or about the same time as the goods being valued shall be the customs value. If, however, more than one transaction value for identical goods is found, the valuation will have to be made on the basis of the lowest amongst them as provided under Rule 5(4). Rule 6 of the Valuation Rules, to determine value of "similar goods", can only be resorted to when price of the imported goods cannot be determined either under Rule 4 or Rule 5 as above. Further, Rule 6(2) states that Rule 5 (2), (3) and (4) shall apply mutatis mutandis for the exercise under Rule 6 as well, thereby, prescribing, inter alia, that the lowest value shall have to be used as the basis of determining the price of the imported goods. Significantly, therefore, the Valuation Rules, following pertinently the general scheme of Article VII of the GATT 1994, expressly stipulates under Rule 5(4) and Rule 6(2) that the lowest value shall be the determinant of the Customs value of the imported goods both in ascertaining the "transaction value" of identical goods -or similar goods respectively. In this regard, these provisions are found, in particular, to correspond wholly with Article 2(3) and Article 3(3) of Article VII of the GATT 1994. 

 (a) Under Rule 3 "transaction value" of any imported item will be its value for the purpose of assessment of Customs/ import duties; 

 (b) Under Rule 4 the declared invoice value paid or payable will be such "transaction value", subject to adjustment made under Rule 10; 

 (c) Only when "transaction value" cannot be determined as above, Rules 5,6,7,8 and 9 can be applied in a strict sequential order to determine value of goods imported; 

 (d) Rule 5 requires, inter cilia, for the lowest value to be the basis for Customs valuation when more than one "transaction value" is found for identical goods and 

 (e) Rule 6 can only be applied when it is not possible to determine value as above under Rules 4 and 5. 

 13. The omnipresence of the above explained provisions and standards of Article VII of the GATT 1994 extends importantly to The PSI Rules as specifically identifies and refers to the Agreement on Implementation of Article VII General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), 1994 as the "Valuation Agreement" under Rule 2(Y). It is noted further that by Rule 2(Z), the PSI Rules also bears specific reference to the Valuation Rules. Under Rule 8 (4), the PSI Rules, it is incumbent upon a PSI agent to determine the value of goods subject to the provisions of Rule 13 therein. Rule 13 ( I ) requires a PSI Agent to determine and certify the value of goods in accordance with the "Valuation Agreement", i.e., Article VII of the GATT 1994. Furthermore, Rule 13(2) requires such PSI agent to provide the concerned exporter the opportunity to sufficiently explain itself in the event that the CRF or the PSI certification denotes a value that is inflated/higher than the invoice value. Rule 22 provides for the usage of the CRF as the basis of assessment of Customs duties. In Out context, Rule 22(3) requires reassessment of price/value by any Customs officer above the rank of an Assistant Commissioner for the purpose of levying Customs duties when it can be confirmed from information received that the CRF value is not the "transaction value". 

 (a) Determining the value of imported goods in accordance with Article VII of the GATT 1994; 

 (b) Providing the concerned exporter an opportunity to submit its statement prior to a CRF being issued with higher valuation than the invoice value and 

 (c) A Customs reassessment of the value of goods as per the .prescription of the Valuation Rules upon confirmation that the CRF valuation does not in all probability reflect the correct price or "transaction value". 

 15. It is noted that under Rule 13 (2) of the PSI Rules, the Petitioner's supplier was never given an opportunity to explain the valuation reflected in the PI as above and consequentially to assert why the CRF certifying a higher valuation should not be issued. Subsequent to the issuance of the CRF, the Petitioner wrote to the Respondent No. 7 PSI Agent on 21.12. 2011 seeking a clarification/explanation on such higher valuation. The response elicited was in the form of a letter dated 22.12.2011 explaining that the valuation was done in accordance with Rule 6 of the Valuation Rules with appropriate adjustments made under Rule 10 of the said Rules. In apparent disregard of the sequential valuation mechanism devised under the Valuation Rules that requires that a Rule 6-valuatioh can only be resorted to if the Customs value is not determinable under Rules 4 and 5, the response of the Respondent No. 7 PSI Agent failed to disclose any information with regard to the justification both for insisting on as well as the resultant process for relying on the "transaction value" of similar goods at a considerably inflated rate as the determinant of Customs value of the goods or why indeed the Respondent No. 7 failed to apply Rules 4 or 5 as is its legal obligation to do under the PSI Rules. 

 16. Relevantly, similar lapses of the Respondent No.7 PSI Agent have incidentally been the subject of consideration and review as prescribed under Rule 23 of the PSI Rules with respect to three other consignments of identical goods imported by the Petitioner, which were also assessed in violation of the PSI Rules read with the Valuation Rules. This Court notes that in all three instances the Review Committee found the valuation of the Respondent No. 7 to be in violation of the Valuation Rules and decided that the Customs value ought to have been assessed on the basis of invoice value instead. Two of the Review Committee's decisions in particular, both dated 24.1.2012, brought on record by the Petitioner are found succinctly to summarize the position in law as above explained to justify the Petitioner's reliance on the declared/invoice/transaction value as the Customs value. In the first such matter, finding on the inaccuracy of the valuation done by the PSI Agent with regard to the Petitioner's consignment imported under Bill of Entry No.C-145336 dated 23.11.2011, the Review Committee pertinently found and decided thus : 

 Notably furthermore, it has not escaped this Court's attention that the fifth and final consignment of the identical goods was assessed by the same Respondent No. 7 at invoice value. That particular consignment of identical goods imported by the Petitioner under B/E No. C-19920 dated 18.2.2012, CRF No. BV 12002e19 dated 30.1.2012 was valued by the Respondent No.4 Assistant Commissioner at an amount higher than the CRF Value. In that CRF, the Respondent No. 7 of PSI Agent of this instant Writ Petition certified the "transaction value" as per Unit price mentioned in the Commercial Invoice. Given that circumstance, the Petitioner on 29.2.2012 applied to the Respondent No.4 for assessing the imported goods as per CRF Value and further on 4.3.2012 the Petitioner, in connection with the said goods, applied to the Respondents No. 4 for releasing the imported goods by accepting bank guarantee covering the difference between the amount of the Customs assessed value and the CRF Value. Upon receiving that application from the Petitioner the Respondent No. 4, it is evident, accepted the said application and accepted the bank guarantee and released the said goods, thereby, as per Rule 22(4) of the PSI Rules. 

 (a) The determination of price of the Goods should have been based on invoice value as per the Valuation Rules as in turn based on Article VII of the GATT 1994; 

 (c) The lowest price on the database maintained by the Respondents for similar or identical goods has not been made the basis of the PSI Agent's verification and certification; 

 (d) The Petitioner's supplier was not informed when the CRF was issued certifying a higher valuation than the invoice value in violation of Rule 13 (2) of the PSI Rules and 

 (e) Subsequent Review Committee decisions and the actions of the PSI Agent itself in assessing the Petitioner's identical goods -at invoice value, further substantiate the fact that the instant assessment and CRF was based on an arbitrary assessment of the Goods wholly in violation of the applicable law. 

 18. Given the findings above, this Court also finds substance in Mr. Sami's arguments that certain consequential avenues are open to the Petitioner to secure a due and early release of the goods. Here, this Court has considered Rule 22 of the PSI Rules which provides that a CRF issued by a PSI agent that conforms to Rule 12-requirements shall be the basis of assessment of customs duties. However, Rule 22 (3) provides that in the event where it can be confirmed by the Customs Authority from the data obtained or information received that the CRF issued by the PSI Agent does not reflect the correct "transaction value", then an officer not below the rank of Assistant Commission of Customs shall have to reassess the value of the goods for the purpose of levying appropriate Customs duties. Furthermore, under Rule 22(4) of the PSI Rules, in the event an importer is not agreeable to pay in cash the Customs duties assessed on the basis of a disputed valuation, and if the importer is willing to furnish a bank guarantee in the amount of the Customs duties payable on the basis of the disputed valuation, the Customs duties will have to be provisionally assessed and goods will have to be released upon furnishing of the said bank guarantee. Indeed, under Rule 22(4), if goods are released against a bank guarantee, the importer will have to submit its case before the Review Committee under Rule 23 (2) of the PSI Rules within twenty-one days, failing which on the twenty-second day the bank guarantee is liable to be cashed. Clearly, therefore, any importer who is either aggrieved by a CRF valuation or temporary assessment under Rule 22(4) of the PSI Rules can come before the Review Committee under Rule 23(2) of the PSI Rules only after having the goods released. Bearing in mind these provisions of the PSI Rules, the Petitioner wrote to the Respondents on 26.1.2012 highlighting the discrepancy between the "transaction value" and the CRF value and requested the Respondents to release the Goods upon a provisional assessment and by accepting a bank guarantee. This, as earlier stated, failed to elicit any response from the Customs Authority, thereby, necessitating the filing of this Application. 

 19. Applying the relevant provisions of both the PSI Rules and the Valuation Rules read with those of the Act relied upon by the Petitioner, and given the evidently arbitrary assessment of the CRF valuation, this Court finds that as mandated in law the Respondents shall have to reevaluate the valuation of the Goods under Rule 22(3). Given this Court's satisfaction that as warranted in the facts and circumstances the Customs Authority can presently indeed arrive at a final decision as to the valuation of the Goods applying the standards and principles as elaborately enunciated above, there is found no justifiable ground to Order instead a mere provisional assessment of the Goods. This Court, accordingly, directs the Customs Authority to strictly so proceed, thereby, necessarily 'allowing the Petitioner to pay the Customs duties as assessed by the Respondents under Rule 23(2) in accordance with the Valuation Rules read in the context of Section 25(1) and (2) of the Act and on the basis of the declared/invoice/transaction value by way of final assessment. 

 20. This Court has found and directed as above upon full satisfaction that in the facts and circumstances both the Respondent No. 7 PSI Agent and the Respondent No. 4 Assistant Commissioner have acted in flagrant violation of mandatorily applicable principles add standards of valuation. The arbitrariness evident in their actions is manifested in the fact that the law in this case is marked more by its breach than in its compliance. In reiteration this Court declarers that the Customs Authority in particular acted most illegally and arbitrarily by failing to comply with Rule 22(3) and not undertaking reassessment of valuation for levying appropriate Customs duties on the Goods. That failure is compounded further by the failure to accept a bank guarantee to secure a release of the Goods when at all material times it could readily be confirmed from the data available at the time of assessment of duties that the CRF value is indeed not the correct "transaction value". 

 21. The learned Assistant Attorney General Ms. Kashefa Hussain has argued, by reference to an Affidavit-in-Opposition, that the Respondents have already "assessed" the Goods in "accordance with law" and there is, therefore, no question of any further amendment. She further submits that the Petitioner's allegation that Rule 22(4) of the PSI Rules has not been complied with is false and reflects an attempt to misinterpret the Rules. She submits that Rule 22(4) presupposes certain circumstances which are described in Rule 22(2) and (3) but those circumstances do not necessarily exist in the instant Case and, therefore, the question of violation of Rule 22(4) in the instant matter does not even arise. Further, denying any significance to be attached to the above cited decisions/determinations of the Review Committee, Ms. Hussain argues that no vested right has accrued to the Petitioner with regard to the instant consignment by reason of the said decisions of the Review Committee. This Court finds these arguments of learned Assistant Attorney General to be unacceptable given that these are premised on a disregard of the true import and purport of the scheme of valuation explained above. Equally unacceptable is the Respondents' stance that the Review Committee's decision in these facts can be of no persuasive or precedential value at all. That, in this Court's view, is tantamount to denying such Rule 23(2) determination process under the PSI Rules of any legal justification and efficacy. Surely, the Respondents, upon proper reflection, will realize the fallacy in such argument made through their Affidavit-in-Opposition. 

 22. Upon a consideration of the above, this Court, therefore, finds that the above assessment of the Goods covered under L/C number 074211010387 dated 20.11.2011 lying under B/E No. C 3489 dated 9.1.2012 on the basis of CRF No. BV 11 l ff862 dated 14.12.2011 valuation at a higher inflated rate ignoring the "transaction value" has indeed been done without lawful authority and is to be deemed to be of no legal effect. Consequentially, the Customs authority, in general, is, hereby, directed to finally assess and release the Goods under the above stated Bill of Entry on the basis of the declared invoice/transaction value within a period of 1 (one) week from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this Judgment and Order.
